source.title: Multi-Epoch Learning for Deep Click-Through Rate Prediction Models
source.authors: Zhaocheng Liu; Zhongxiang Fan; Jian Liang; Dongying Kong; Han Li

record.file_problem: The full paper is present, but some table and figure layout is flattened, and the text contains inconsistent placeholder conference metadata.
record.tranche_reason: The paper measures test metrics over training epochs in deep CTR models, using a different setting and measures from the original double-descent work.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results on test AUC and test loss across epochs, so those bear on V2. Training metrics in Figure 2 are excluded because V2 concerns test error. The reduced-data experiment is recorded under fits_no_version: it changes sample count but does not test whether more data raises test error near an interpolation threshold. The paper's method comparisons and online A/B results do not measure the claimed epoch-wise curve.
record.test_reason: This is a CTR method paper proposing MEDA, which reinitializes embeddings each epoch. It cites Belkin et al. only in a list of overfitting references and never examines double descent. Its epoch-wise results show either one-epoch overfitting (a single drop in performance after epoch 1) or the gains from its own method. No model-size, sample-size or capacity sweep is run, and there is no check for a second descent. The results therefore measure a different construct (one-epoch overfitting) or the method's own performance, not any version of the claim.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that reinitializing embeddings each epoch (MEDA) avoids embedding overfitting, so multi-epoch training beats one-epoch training. They also report that most MEDA models improve steadily in test AUC over 8 epochs, and they cite online A/B gains on Kuaishou. They attribute standard one-epoch overfitting to sparse embeddings and make no claim about double descent.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses CTR architectures and AUC/loss across epochs, and proposes embedding reinitialization (MEDA); it does not reproduce the original double-descent sweeps.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported epoch trends differ between ordinary training and MEDA; results also vary across CTR models and datasets.

fits_no_version.finding: In standard multi-epoch training, deep CTR models (shown for DNN on Taobao) degrade sharply at the start of the second epoch, so the best test performance comes after one epoch.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Deep CTR models with sparse embeddings show one-epoch overfitting, a single post-epoch-1 degradation attributed to embedding overfitting.

record.problems: No uncertainty estimates are reported. Several epoch-wise results are presented only in figures, and the text gives only an aggregate trend for the majority of models. The one-epoch comparison with MEDA also changes the training method, so it cannot isolate the effect of epoch count.
record.rows_left_out: Training loss and training AUC curves in Figure 2 were left out because the claim versions concern test error. No model-specific rows were extracted from Figure 4 because the text reports only an aggregate majority trend and the plotted values are figure-only.

untested.parts: All of V1: there is no model-size sweep.
All of V2: there is no analysis of a fall-rise-fall test-error trajectory in ordinary training.
All of V3: the reduced-data runs use the MEDA method and involve no interpolation threshold.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's challenges label on V2 is removed. Row r15 measures the study's own method's trajectory, not epoch-wise double descent arising in ordinary training. The paper's subject is one-epoch overfitting, a related but distinct construct. The original sources' reference (Belkin et al.) appears only as a citation.

versions.untested_parts: Model-size scaling and a peak near the size that just fits the training set.
The paper measures epoch-wise test metrics, but does not establish a full fall-rise-fall curve or locate a peak relative to the epoch at which the training set is just fit.
The reduced-data experiment does not test whether increasing sample size near an interpolation threshold raises test error.
No general capacity sweep across model classes or interpolation-point analysis.
No single effective-complexity measure is evaluated across size, epochs, or sample count.
No test of label-noise or variance dependence, multiple peaks, or optimally tuned regularization.
No alternative effective-parameter count or re-expression of the curve.

rows.subject: Base+MEDA models (majority aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Train base CTR models with MEDA for up to 8 epochs
rows.value: The majority of models show a stable upward trend as epochs increase
rows.note: The authors report the trend for a majority, not model-by-model; this does not describe the fall-rise-fall pattern in those tested MEDA runs.
rows.check: This is the MEDA method's performance across epochs, an ablation of the study's own method. It cannot challenge V2, so it should not be marked absent. Table 2 also shows AUC falling at higher epoch counts for some models, so the trend is not purely upward.

rows.subject: Base CTR models (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Train with reduced fractions of the Taobao data and assess epochs needed to recover the full-data one-epoch result
rows.measure: Epochs to recover the effect of one-epoch training on complete data; Test AUC
rows.baseline: One-epoch training on complete Taobao data
rows.value: MEDA recovers that effect within 16 epochs
rows.note: This is an aggregate statement about sample utilization; it does not test sample-size effects near an interpolation threshold.
rows.check: This is a sample-efficiency result for the study's own method. The value is also imprecise: Table 2 gives per-model epochs and AUC for each data fraction, for example DNN 12.5% needs 7 epochs to reach 0.8716.
